title: One Neuron in Separate Chambers
endLine: Separate cell body and axon fluids to test where signals act.

scenes.tts: When a neuron needs a signal, which end must touch it? Developing sympathetic neurons need nerve growth factor, or N G F, to survive. In an ordinary dish, one fluid bathes the cell body and its long axons. So you cannot tell which part needs the factor.
scenes.caption: When a neuron needs a signal, which end must touch it? Developing sympathetic neurons need nerve growth factor, or NGF, to survive. In an ordinary dish, one fluid bathes the cell body and its long axons. So you cannot tell which part needs the factor.
scenes.visual: Schematic overhead view of one culture dish filling most of the frame height; a sympathetic neuron extends long axons across the dish inside one uniform bath of slowly drifting NGF dots; question marks pulse gently over both the cell body and the far axon tips (schematic, no molecular structures).
scenes.narration: When a neuron needs a signal, which end must touch it? Developing sympathetic neurons need nerve growth factor, or NGF, to survive. In an ordinary dish, one fluid bathes the cell body and its long axons. So you cannot tell which part needs the factor.

scenes.visual: The same schematic dish remains live with NGF dots drifting gently; the title "One Neuron in Separate Chambers" fades in cleanly above the dish and clears.

scenes.tts: In 1977, Robert Campenot divided one dish into chambers. A barrier sealed to the floor separates a central chamber from side chambers. Rat sympathetic cell bodies sit in the centre; their axons grow under the seal. Because the fluids stay apart, each chamber's bath can change on its own.

scenes.visual: In the same schematic dish, a solid divider lowers and seals to the floor, splitting it into a central chamber and left and right side chambers; rat sympathetic cell bodies settle in the centre and schematic axons grow beneath the seal into both side chambers; fluid tints shift independently in each chamber while stopping cleanly at the sealed barrier (schematic).
scenes.narration: In 1977, Robert Campenot divided one dish into chambers. A barrier sealed to the floor separates a central chamber from side chambers. scenes.tts: Now take N G F away from one side only. Keep it on the central cell bodies and in the right chamber. Drain it from the left chamber alone. What happens to the left branches, and to the same neuron's branches next door?
scenes.caption: Now take NGF away from one side only. Keep it on the central cell bodies and in the right chamber. Drain it from the left chamber alone. What happens to the left branches, and to the same neuron's branches next door?
scenes.visual: In the same three-chamber schematic dish, drifting NGF dots remain in the central and right chambers while fluid drains out of the left side chamber, leaving the left branches bare; a high-contrast question card asks what happens to the left branches and to the same neuron's branches on the right (schematic).
scenes.narration: Now take NGF away from one side only. Keep it on the central cell bodies and in the right chamber. Drain it from the left chamber alone. What happens to the left branches, and to the same neuron's branches next door?

scenes.visual: Thinking pause on the same three-chamber schematic dish with the prediction question still on screen; NGF dots drift slowly in the central and right chambers while the bare left chamber stays still.

scenes.tts: The left axons stop growing and later degenerate, though their cell bodies keep N G F. The same neuron's branches next door stay: pruning in miniature, one branch cut back. Now drain the factor from the centre alone. When only the axons' far ends reach N G F, many cell bodies still survive.
scenes.caption: The left axons stop growing and later degenerate, though their cell bodies keep NGF. The same neuron's branches next door stay: pruning in miniature, one branch cut back. Now drain the factor from the centre alone. When only the axons' far ends reach NGF, many cell bodies still survive.
scenes.visual: In the same schematic dish, the bare left axons stall and break apart while the right branches of the same neuron stay intact; next, NGF drains from the central chamber while staying on the right distal axons, and schematic signal pulses travel back under the seal to keep the central cell bodies illuminated (schematic).
scenes.narration: The left axons stop growing and later degenerate, though their cell bodies keep NGF. The same neuron's branches next door stay: pruning in miniature, one branch cut back. Now drain the factor from the centre alone. When only the axons' far ends reach NGF, many cell bodies still survive.

scenes.tts: Separating the two fluids reveals where a signal acts and whether it travels. Axons grow only where N G F touches them, whatever bathes the cell bodies. Signaling proteins beside the receptor at the tip do some of that local work. Survival is the part that needs the nucleus. So when only the tips touch N G F, a signal must travel home.

scenes.visual: Zoom smoothly on one schematic neuron crossing the barrier in the same dish: a local glow beside the axon tip drives schematic branch extension where NGF dots touch; then, with NGF only at the tip, a separate schematic pulse travels back along the axon into the cell body's nucleus (schematic, no molecular structures; the pulse is unlabelled because what carries the signal is still open).
scenes.narration: Separating the two fluids reveals where a signal acts and whether it travels. Axons grow only where NGF touches them, whatever bathes the cell bodies. Signaling proteins beside the receptor at the tip do some of that local work. Survival is the part that needs the nucleus. So when only the tips touch NGF, a signal must travel home.

scenes.tts: If the seal leaks, fluids mix and hide where a signal acts. Putting a factor straight on cell bodies bypasses the trip. Testing both sides separates local effects from signals sent home. Still, whether N G F itself travels, or a faster signal contributes, stays open. Nor is every arriving signal shown to be enough.

scenes.visual: In the same schematic dish, a brief leak beneath the barrier blends chamber tints together under a warning mark, then seals tightly again; next, an NGF drop onto the cell body shows a bypassed arrow with a slash; finally, two schematic question pulses move along the axon labelled "NGF itself?" and "Faster signal?" (schematic).

scenes.tts: First, Campenot's 1977 dish separated local axon growth from survival signals sent home. Second, Noo Li Jeon developed a small relative, the microfluidic chamber.
scenes.caption: First, Campenot's 1977 dish separated local axon growth from survival signals sent home. Second, Noo Li Jeon developed a small relative, the microfluidic chamber.
scenes.visual: The same schematic three-chamber dish tags "Campenot, 1977" over its two results (left axons degenerate; cell bodies survive on axon NGF), then scales down smoothly into a schematic microfluidic chamber labelled "Noo Li Jeon" (schematic).
scenes.narration: First, Campenot's 1977 dish separated local axon growth from survival signals sent home. Second, Noo Li Jeon developed a small relative, the microfluidic chamber.

scenes.tts: Natasha Sharma and colleagues in David Ghinty's laboratory used it. Their axons got N G F; the receptor for it, track A, carried a tag called Flag. Over six hours, tagged track A appeared as dots in the dendrites, the receiving branches. That was compared with clustering of postsynaptic proteins, on the synapse's receiving side.
scenes.caption: Natasha Sharma and colleagues in David Ginty's laboratory used it. Their axons got NGF; the receptor for it, TrkA, carried a tag called Flag. Over six hours, tagged TrkA appeared as dots in the dendrites, the receiving branches. That was compared with clustering of postsynaptic proteins, on the synapse's receiving side.
scenes.visual: In the schematic microfluidic chamber, the heading changes from "Noo Li Jeon" to "Sharma and colleagues, Ginty laboratory"; schematic NGF dots enter the axon side; glowing dots labelled "Flag-TrkA" appear in the dendrites as a schematic six-hour dial advances, beside schematic postsynaptic clusters shown for comparison (schematic, no molecular structures).

scenes.tts: Third, Phillip Nelson's laboratory used compartmented nerve-muscle cultures. Protein kinase C, or P K C, mediated heterosynaptic loss, where activity at one input costs its less active neighbour. Protein kinase A, or P K A, stabilized the stimulated input. Both acted through acetylcholine receptor numbers at the synapse. Dividing a neuron's bath shows where signals act and whether they travel.
scenes.caption: Third, Phillip Nelson's laboratory used compartmented nerve-muscle cultures. scenes.visual: The compartmented dish transforms smoothly into a schematic nerve-muscle chamber labelled "Phillip Nelson's laboratory": two schematic axons meet one muscle cell; the stimulated axon keeps dense schematic acetylcholine receptor dots under a "PKA" label while the less active neighbour loses receptor dots and fades away under a "PKC" label (schematic, no molecular structures).
